subtitle: Study Tema Okun's characteristics of white supremacy culture as one reflective lens on organizational norms: where the framework came from, what it can and cannot show, its strengths and published critiques, and how to use it on a process without labeling a person.
audience: For DHS and DSD staff, supervisors, managers, policy leads and facilitators who have met Okun's framework in training or discussion and want to use it carefully, or who want to understand the debate about it before deciding how it fits their work.

lessons.title: Where the framework came from, and what it claims
objectives: Describe the origins of Okun's framework and how it has been revised since the original 1999 list.
Explain what Okun says the framework is for and is not for.
Distinguish a characteristic of a culture from a judgment about a person's identity, character or motive.
Locate the current version of the framework and its companion Racial Equity Principles before relying on an older copy.
lessons.teaching:
Many DHS and DSD staff have met Tema Okun's list in a training handout, a slide or a meeting, often as a single page with no explanation of where it came from. That page usually traces back to an essay Okun wrote in 1999 after a difficult antiracism workshop. It was published in 2001 as part of Dismantling Racism: A Workbook for Social Change Groups, which Okun developed with Kenneth Jones, a mentor, and other contributors. The original list named fifteen characteristics, including perfectionism, sense of urgency, defensiveness, quantity over quality, worship of the written word, only one right way, paternalism, either/or thinking, power hoarding, fear of open conflict, individualism, progress defined as bigger or more, objectivity and the right to comfort. The essay paired the characteristics with suggested antidotes, practical counter-habits a group could try.

Okun has said plainly that the original list was not the result of research. It came from years of organizing, workshops and reflection, and it spread online largely without the workbook that gave it context. In May 2021 Okun published a revised version as a website, White Supremacy Culture: Still Here. In a 2023 interview Okun described that revision as adding attention to social class, capitalism and Christian hegemony, and the site gives more attention to fear and to how forms of power intersect. The website has continued to change; the version cited in this course is dated 2025. Okun has asked people to stop circulating the 1999 list and to use the newer material instead, beginning with the Racial Equity Principles on the same site. If the copy in your files is a single undated page, it is probably the version its author has asked people to retire.

What does the framework claim? Its subject is culture: the standards, habits and assumptions an institution treats as normal and neutral, and how those defaults can reflect a history of racial hierarchy about whose ways of working count as professional. It does not claim that every white person shares these habits, that people of color do not, or that a single habit proves anyone holds racist beliefs. In the same 2023 interview Okun described the list as an internal map for looking at yourself and your organization, not a checklist for assessing or targeting someone. Okun said it is not meant to be used to target people, called the idea that asking for a written report is worship of the written word absurd, and separated perfectionism from excellence; high standards are not the concern.

That gives three working rules for this course. First, the framework is a lens for asking questions about norms, not a verdict about a person, a team or a decision. Second, it is one lens among several. Other modules in this pathway draw on Edgar Schein's work on the assumptions underneath culture, Peter Senge's systems thinking, Kimberlé Crenshaw's work on intersectionality and Sins Invalid's disability justice principles. Third, a lens raises a question that local evidence has to answer. Whether a deadline, a writing standard or a decision process is creating an avoidable barrier in DSD work depends on what the rule requires, how it works for the people who must use it, and what other explanations are plausible. The framework helps you notice; it does not do the checking for you.
lessons.keyPoint: Okun's framework is a reflective lens on organizational culture, revised by its author since 1999. It raises questions about norms; it does not diagnose people, and local evidence still has to answer the questions it raises.
lessons.example: Practice case: At a team meeting, {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} shares a one-page handout from a previous job that lists the original fifteen characteristics with no date or source. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} says the list helped explain why the old workplace felt exhausting and suggests the DSD team use it to review its own habits. {{CASE_MANAGER}} says the list feels like it is calling the team racist for caring about deadlines. {{SUPERVISOR}} wants to keep the useful part of the suggestion without letting the conversation turn into a debate about people.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} do next?
choices: Adopt the handout as written and ask each team member to mark which characteristics describe them.
Set the suggestion aside, since the framework is controversial and the team has other priorities.
Thank both colleagues, explain that the author has revised the list and asked people to use the newer version, and propose using it to examine one team process rather than individuals.
feedback: Asking people to mark which characteristics describe them turns a cultural lens into a personal checklist, which is the use Okun warns against. It also relies on a version the author has asked people to retire.

Dropping the idea dismisses an experience that a colleague found clarifying and avoids a question the team could examine productively. Controversy is a reason to use the framework carefully, not a reason to ignore it.
This respects both reactions, corrects the source, and points the lens at a process the team owns. It keeps the conversation on norms and evidence instead of on who is or is not at fault.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall the first time you encountered Okun's list, or use the practice case. What version did you see, what context came with it, and how did that shape your first reaction to it?
lessons.action: Find any copy of the Okun list your team or training materials use. Note its date and source. Compare it with the current website and the Racial Equity Principles, and write two sentences on what is different.

check.question: How does Okun describe the intended use of her framework?
check.correct: As an internal map for examining yourself and your organization's culture, not a checklist for assessing or targeting a person.
wrong: As a validated research instrument for measuring a workplace's level of racism.
As a list of behaviors that, when observed, prove a colleague holds racist beliefs.
check.feedback: Okun has said the original list was not the result of research and was not meant to target people. Its value is in prompting reflection about cultural norms, which then has to be checked against evidence about a specific process.

lessons.title: Strengths and critiques, weighed fairly
objectives: Explain what the framework does well, including making invisible norms visible and supporting reflection.
Summarize the main published critiques: limited empirical foundation, concerns about essentialist definitions, and misuse in organizations.
Identify which critiques Okun herself shares and which remain points of disagreement.
Decide how the strengths and critiques should shape the way a team uses the framework.
lessons.teaching:
A framework used as widely as Okun's deserves both a fair account of why people value it and an honest account of why others object to it. Presenting only one side would weaken trust in the course and in the framework. The strengths are real. The framework gives names to habits that many people experience but find hard to describe, such as a pace that leaves no room to ask the people affected, or a standard of polish that quietly decides whose contributions are heard. Naming a habit makes it discussable. The list also invites people to examine their own organizations, and the antidotes and Racial Equity Principles point toward practice rather than blame. In a 2023 roundtable published by The Forge, a journal for organizers, several racial justice leaders said the essay resonated because it gave a frame to painful workplace experiences, and one called it useful for reflection.

The critiques are also real, and some come from people who share the framework's goals. The first concerns evidence. The original list was not researched, and we found no peer-reviewed study that tests whether these characteristics describe organizations or whether using the list improves them. It should be treated as a practice-based reflection tool, not as research. The second concerns definitions. Participants in the same Forge roundtable argued that tying habits like urgency or writing to whiteness risks essentialism, the idea that a racial group shares fixed traits. One participant called the framing a false syllogism. Another warned that it can reify race, and some suggested other tools, such as polarity mapping, that examine trade-offs and power without that framing. Many of the listed habits appear across cultures and can be useful in proportion.

The third critique concerns what happens when the list is used in organizations. In a widely read 2022 essay, Maurice Mitchell, national director of the Working Families Party, wrote that decontextualized or uncritical use of the essay had at times been used to challenge accountability around metrics, timeliness and written communication. Mitchell noted that these are not in and of themselves examples of white supremacy. Roundtable participants described the list being weaponized against leaders of color in particular, and one called it a very poor tool for assessing workplace relations. Okun agrees that misuse is widespread. In 2023 Okun said the misuse was heartbreaking and asked people to stop using the list to target anyone. Where Okun and the critics still differ is mainly over the framing itself and how useful the tool can be for management.

For DHS and DSD work, the fair conclusion is neither adoption nor dismissal. Use the framework for what it does well: surfacing norms, prompting self-examination and opening questions about whose ways of working are treated as standard. Guard against its documented risks by keeping it attached to a specific process, pairing it with other lenses and with evidence, and refusing to use it as a label for a person. Public service also has legitimate obligations, such as legal deadlines, accurate records, program integrity and data, that the framework does not erase. A good use of the lens can explain both why a deadline matters and why the way it is set might be shutting people out.
lessons.keyPoint: The framework's strengths are in naming norms and prompting reflection. Its critiques concern evidence, essentialist definitions and misuse. Use it attached to a process, beside other lenses, and never as a label.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is planning a half-day workshop for a DSD policy unit and is considering whether to include Okun's framework. {{CASE_MANAGER}}, who joined from a county, says a facilitator once used it there and it helped the team rethink a rushed review process. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} has read critiques that the framework lacks evidence and has been used to shut down disagreement, and worries that including it will divide the unit.
lessons.question: Which plan best reflects both the strengths and the critiques?
choices: Include the framework with its origins, author's cautions and published critiques, pair it with another lens, and apply it to one real unit process with clear ground rules about not labeling people.
Present the framework as settled knowledge so the session does not get sidetracked by debate.
Leave the framework out entirely and use only tools with empirical validation.
feedback: This gives staff enough context to judge the tool, uses it for reflection on a process, and builds in protections against the misuse that critics and the author both describe.
Presenting a practice-based tool as settled knowledge overstates the evidence and invites the backlash that critics describe. Staff who know the critiques may stop trusting the rest of the session.
Empirical rigor matters, but many useful reflection tools are practice-based. Excluding the framework entirely also leaves staff without guidance when they meet it elsewhere, which they likely will.
lessons.reflection: Privately note which critique of the framework you find most persuasive and which strength you find most useful. If you have only heard one side before, what changes when you hold both?
lessons.action: Write a short paragraph you could use to introduce the framework to a colleague. Include where it came from, one strength, one published critique, and one ground rule for using it on a process rather than a person.

check.question: Which statement fairly describes the evidence base for Okun's framework?
check.correct: It is a practice-based reflection tool; its author says the original was not researched, and we found no peer-reviewed study validating it.
wrong: It is a validated diagnostic instrument developed through large workplace studies.
It has been disproven, so any use of it is unsupported.
check.feedback: The framework draws on practice and reflection rather than research. That limits what it can establish, but it does not make it useless as a prompt for questions that local evidence can then test.

lessons.title: From characteristics to principles and cultural tensions
objectives: Explain the purpose of antidotes and of Okun's Racial Equity Principles as companions to the characteristics.
Describe the Cultural Tensions in Public Service reframing and its six pairs.
Analyze what each side of a tension protects and what happens when one side always dominates.
Apply a tension to a DSD process to identify who benefits and who carries the cost.
lessons.teaching:
A list of problems only takes a team so far. From the start, Okun's work paired each characteristic with antidotes, practices a group could try instead, and Okun now points readers first to the Racial Equity Principles, which describe ways of sharing power, practicing accountability and working more equitably. The design lesson is that the characteristics are most useful as a prompt to ask what a healthier practice would look like. For example, a team that recognizes a pattern of manufactured urgency can ask what a realistic timeline would require, which deadlines are fixed by law or by people waiting for services, and where time for input could be protected. A team that recognizes perfectionism can ask how it treats mistakes and whether people feel able to say they are struggling.

This pathway also uses a reframing called Cultural Tensions in Public Service. It responds to a fair critique: many of the habits on Okun's list are useful in proportion. A sense of urgency gets a service authorized before someone loses housing. Standardization helps make sure similar cases are treated alike. Expertise keeps a policy within the law. The reframing names six pairs that public agencies have to hold together: efficiency and participation, expertise and lived experience, standardization and accessibility, productivity and well-being, control and shared leadership, and speed and thoughtfulness. Each side protects something real. The problem the lens points to is not either value; it is what happens when one side always wins, so that the other stops being considered at all.

Working with a tension starts with four questions. What does each side protect in this process? What do we see when the first side dominates, for example decisions made before affected people can respond, or a form so standardized that some people cannot complete it? What would we see if the other side dominated instead, such as endless consultation that delays a needed change? And who carries the cost of the current balance? This last question links the lens to the anti-racism questions running through this pathway: who benefits, who is burdened, whose voice matters, who belongs and who is excluded. A tension that always resolves the same way usually resolves in favor of the people who designed the process.

The reframing does not replace Okun's analysis of power, and it should not become a way to make every concern sound like a neutral trade-off. Some imbalances reflect who holds authority and whose knowledge has been discounted, and naming that plainly is part of the work. The reframing helps a mixed team discuss a norm without starting from accusation, and it keeps legitimate obligations in view. Some participants in the 2023 Forge roundtable recommended polarity mapping and similar tools for this reason: they make trade-offs and power visible together. In DSD work, the practical result might be a review timeline that keeps a required effective date and also reserves a fixed window for self-advocates and lead agencies to respond.
lessons.keyPoint: Antidotes and the Racial Equity Principles turn the characteristics toward practice. The Cultural Tensions reframing asks what each side protects, what happens when one side always dominates, and who carries the cost.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD team has six weeks to issue guidance to lead agencies on a program change with a fixed effective date. In past cycles, the team drafted and finalized guidance internally, then sent it out. Lead agencies and self-advocates have said the guidance often arrives with steps that do not match how services work locally. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} says there is no time for outside review. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, a county case management lead, has offered to convene a small review group within a week.
lessons.question: How can the team use the speed and thoughtfulness tension here?
choices: Delay the guidance until every lead agency has had a full comment period, since thoughtfulness should come first.
Keep the effective date, name what speed protects and what has been lost when it always wins, and build a short, fixed review window with the offered group into the timeline.
Keep the internal-only process, since the deadline is fixed and outside input is a preference rather than a requirement.
feedback: This lets the other side of the tension dominate. Missing a fixed effective date would create its own harm for the people the change affects.
This holds both values. It respects the real deadline, takes seriously the evidence that internal-only drafting has left gaps, and gives the people who carry those gaps a defined role.
This lets speed win again by default. The team has evidence that the current balance creates costs for lead agencies and the people they serve, and an offer that fits inside the timeline.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider which of the six tensions shows up most often in your work, or use the practice case. Which side usually wins, and who would you need to hear from to know what that costs?
lessons.action: Choose one recurring process. Name the tension most at play, write one sentence on what each side protects, and note one sign that one side has been winning by default. Share the note with a colleague who works on the same process.

check.question: According to the Cultural Tensions reframing, when does a value such as efficiency or standardization become a problem?
check.correct: When it always wins, so that the value on the other side, such as participation or accessibility, stops being considered.
wrong: Whenever it is used at all, because these values are harmful in themselves.
Only when someone can prove that a person intended to exclude others.
check.feedback: Each side of a tension protects something real. The lens asks what happens when one side dominates by default, and who carries the cost, without requiring proof of intent.

lessons.title: Using the lens on a process without labeling a person
objectives: Apply a step-by-step method for examining a process through the lens using observable evidence.
Rephrase a statement that labels a person into one that describes a process and its effects.
Connect a characteristic to the related domain in this pathway, such as Belonging, Accessibility, Leadership or Well-Being.
Plan a change and a way to study its effects on the work rather than on people.
lessons.teaching:
The most common misuse of the framework is also the easiest to slip into: hearing a characteristic and attaching it to a person. 'They are power hoarding' or 'that is just their perfectionism' sounds like analysis but works as a label. It invites defensiveness, says nothing about what to change, and can be applied unfairly, as critics have documented. The same observation can be described as a process. 'Decisions about this form are made before the people who use it can respond' points to a step that can be examined and changed. The habit to build is translating: from a trait to a pattern, from a person to a step, from a motive to an effect. Okun's own suggestion to use the framework first as an internal map applies here too. It is often most useful when you start with your own habits and your own team's routines.

A practical method follows five steps. First, name the process and its purpose, including any requirement fixed by law, rule or contract. Second, describe what you observe, in terms another person could check: who is invited, how input arrives, how long people have, what happens to a question. Third, choose the characteristic or tension that best illuminates a question about it, and say the question plainly. Fourth, gather evidence and consider other explanations, including workload, unclear authority or a system limitation. Ask who benefits, who is burdened and whose voice is missing. Fifth, decide what is within your role. A staff member can raise a pattern with the person who owns the process. A supervisor can change a meeting practice. A manager can revise criteria or protect time for review. A concern about a specific person's conduct is different; it belongs with the supervisor, Human Resources or the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division, not with a team reflection exercise.

The lens also connects to other domains in this pathway, which helps a team choose where to look. Perfectionism, sense of urgency, defensiveness and quantity over quality often show up first as Culture questions about how work gets done. Fear, right to comfort and either/or thinking connect to Belonging: whether people can speak up, have difficult conversations and hold more than one view. Perfectionism, worship of the written word and only one right way connect to Accessibility, which Module 4 takes up. Power hoarding, paternalism, individualism and claims of objectivity connect to Leadership and how decisions are shared. Urgency, perfectionism, quantity over quality and fear connect to Well-Being and the pace people can sustain.

Finally, decide how you will know whether anything changed. Success here is measured in the work, not in people: a notice that more people understand on the first read, a decision with its reasons written down, a barrier removed from a request process, community input that led to a documented change. This course does not track or score anyone, and finishing it is not evidence that a team has changed. Use a short cycle of plan, try, study and adjust. Plan one change with an owner and a date to look again. Try it. Study what happened, including any new burden it created. Adjust, and tell the people who contributed what changed and what did not.
lessons.keyPoint: Translate from a trait to a pattern, from a person to a step, and from a motive to an effect. Measure change in the work, not in people, and route conduct concerns to the responsible office.
lessons.example: Practice case: After a frustrating planning meeting, {{CASE_MANAGER}} tells {{SUPERVISOR}} privately that a senior colleague 'is power hoarding,' because the colleague finalized the project timeline before anyone else could comment. {{CASE_MANAGER}} wants {{SUPERVISOR}} to share Okun's framework with the colleague. {{SUPERVISOR}} knows the timeline was set quickly because of a leadership request, and also knows that the team has raised concerns before about decisions arriving already made.
lessons.question: What is the best response from {{SUPERVISOR}}?
choices: Acknowledge the concern, reframe it as a question about how project timelines get set, and propose a step that gives the team a defined chance to respond before timelines are final.
Forward the framework to the senior colleague with a note that the team has noticed power hoarding.
Explain that the timeline came from leadership, so there is nothing to discuss.
feedback: This takes the concern seriously while moving it from a label to a process the supervisor can influence. It also uses what the supervisor knows about the timeline's origin instead of assuming a motive.
Sending the framework as a verdict about one person is the misuse the author and critics warn against. It will likely produce defensiveness and leave the process unchanged.
The leadership request explains this one timeline, but not the recurring pattern the team has raised. Closing the conversation misses a process question the supervisor can address.
lessons.reflection: Privately write down one judgment you have made, or heard, that attached a characteristic to a person. How would you restate it as a description of a process and its effects?
lessons.action: Use the job aid to examine one process you work in. Name the process, the observable pattern, the characteristic or tension that frames your question, the evidence you would gather, who can decide, one change to try and a date to study its effects.

check.question: Which statement uses the lens on a process rather than labeling a person?
check.correct: Timelines for this project have been final before the team could comment; can we add a review step?
wrong: Our lead is showing power hoarding again.
That kind of perfectionism comes from the culture that colleague grew up in.
check.feedback: Describing an observable pattern in a process points to something the team can examine and change. Attaching a characteristic to a person, or to a person's background, labels them and predicts behavior from identity.

cards.back: A practice-based lens, first written in 1999 and revised as a website in 2021, that names cultural norms an institution can treat as neutral. It raises questions; it does not diagnose people.
Okun's description of the intended use: a way to examine your own habits and your organization's culture, not a tool to assess or target a person.
Companions to the characteristics that point toward practice. Okun recommends starting with the Racial Equity Principles.
Makes invisible norms visible and discussable, and supports reflection and self-assessment in organizations.
A limited empirical foundation, concerns that some definitions are essentialist, and documented misuse to label people or resist accountability.
Two values public service must hold together, such as speed and thoughtfulness. The concern is when one side always wins and the other stops being considered.
From a trait to a pattern, from a person to a step, from a motive to an effect.
A short cycle for testing a change in a process and measuring its effect on the work, not on people.

aid.heading: Check the source and frame
items: Use the current website and Racial Equity Principles, not an undated copy of the 1999 list.
Introduce the framework with its origins, one strength and one critique.
Agree that the lens applies to processes and norms, not to people.

aid.heading: Describe the process
items: Name the process, its purpose and any requirement fixed by law, rule or contract.
Describe what you observe in terms someone else could check.
Choose the characteristic or tension that best frames a question, and write the question.

aid.heading: Weigh the tension and the evidence
items: Write what each side of the tension protects.
Ask who benefits, who is burdened, whose voice matters and who is excluded.
Consider other explanations, such as workload, unclear authority or system limits.
Send concerns about a specific person's conduct to the supervisor, Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division.

aid.heading: Change and study
items: Choose one change within your role, with an owner and a date to look again.
Measure the effect on the work, such as clearer notices, documented reasons or a barrier removed.
Tell contributors what changed and what did not.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: The primary framework in its current website form. Okun describes it as an analytical tool, cautions against using it to accuse people, and distinguishes high standards from perfectionism. The framework draws on practice and reflection; the original list was not an empirical diagnostic instrument.

sources.title: Tema Okun, Racial Equity Principles
sources.note: Companion principles for shared power, accountability and more equitable ways of working, which the author recommends as a starting point. They are practice guidance, not research findings.

sources.title: The Intercept, Deconstructed podcast: Tema Okun on Her Mythical Paper on White Supremacy (February 3, 2023)
sources.note: Interview in which Okun describes the framework as an internal map rather than a checklist, acknowledges widespread misuse, separates excellence from perfectionism and asks people to use the 2021 revision. It records the author's own account, not independent evidence about the framework.

sources.title: The Forge, How (Not) to Dismantle White Supremacy (April 20, 2023)
sources.note: A roundtable of racial justice leaders discussing both the essay's resonance and its limits, including concerns about essentialism, weaponization and fit for management, with suggestions such as polarity mapping. It presents practitioner views, not research.

sources.title: Maurice Mitchell, Building Resilient Organizations (The Forge, November 29, 2022)
sources.note: An essay on organizational culture in progressive organizations that notes how uncritical use of the Okun essay has been used to challenge accountability for metrics, timeliness and writing. It is an informed practitioner perspective, not a study.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency policy on considering equity in daily work and using the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions. This course is learning material and does not substitute for the policy.

sources.title: State of Minnesota, Equity Analysis Toolkit
sources.note: A state-government resource for asking who is affected, engaging people meaningfully and reviewing equity impacts in a decision. It supports the process steps in this course rather than the Okun framework itself.
